full_judgment:
2. Late Eklas Hossain Khan predecessor of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 made an application under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption of the case land measuring 0.0206 acre of C.S. and S.A. plot No. 565 appertaining to S. A. Khatian No. 612 and Mutation Khatian No. 474/18. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that the case land along with other lands originally belonged to Jogesh Chandra Majumder and others and the C.S. record of rights was accordingly prepared and published in their names. Golam Mortuza Khan, father of the pre-emptor and opposite party Nos. 3-11 purchased 5 kathas of land by registered deed of sale from the said tenants and lived there by constructing dwelling house and on payment of rents on mutation in his own name. Thereafter Golam Mortuza Khan died leaving pre-emptor and opposite party Nos. 3-5 as four sons and opposite party Nos. 6-11 as six daughters and the said heirs possessed the lands jointly by way of inheritance. Opposite party No. 4 by registered deed of sale dated 18.02.88 transferred his share to his brother opposite party No. 3 and delivered possession. Opposite party No. 3 transferred the said land by a deed of sale executed on the same date to the petitioner and the deed of sale was registered on 13.08.88. In spite of the fact that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer in the joint tenancy no notice was served upon him. The pre-emptor was in possession in the house constructed by him. 

 6. On the pleadings issues framed are whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy, whether the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation, whether there was any improvement made by the purchase and what relief or reliefs the pre-emptor is entitled to. 

 8. On consideration of the evidence on record the trial court held that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer of the tenancy, that the application for pre-emption is barred by limitation and that there is a proof of development of the case land by purchaser. Upon such view, the trial court dismissed the application for pre-emption. 

 10. Mr. N. H. Khondker appearing for the purchaser submits that in view of provision of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the appellate court failed to take into consideration the findings of the trial court and reasons given for those and without considering the evidence on record held that the pre-emptor is a co-sharer of the tenancy and the application for pre-emption is not barred by limitation. In support of his submission he also cited the cases reported in 5 BLD (AD) 54, 15 BLD (AD) 91, 16 BLD (AD) 197 and 17 BLD (AD) 47. 

 11. The learned Advocate also submits that the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters were separated by amicable partition among them and had been enjoying separate jama since then and the Municipal holding also shows that the pre-emptor was enjoying his share separately in separate holding number. The Court of appeal below therefore, committed serious error of law in riot considering those facts incoming to its decision. I-le further submits that after purchase he also got his purchased land mutated and he has been paying rent through his mutated Khatian since purchase and also staying there after constructing a semi-pucca house and installing all modern utility services, namely, electricity, gas, WASA etc. Even after such independent and separate enjoyment of the purchased land, the finding of the appellate court that tenancy was riot separated is totally misconceived and not sanctioned by any law. 

 13. Mr. Abdul Barek Chowdhury appearing for the opposite Party Nos. 1 and 2, submits that only two questions are involved in the case as to limitation and whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy out of which that land was sold. On limitation, he submits that the impugned kabala was finally registered on 13.08.88 and application was filed on 25.09.88 so it cannot be said that application for pre-emption was beyond the time, no matter the certified copy of the application was obtained on 16.03.88. On the issue of locus standi as co-sharer, he submits that as no order of any competent authority could be adduced by the purchaser to show that the tenancy was ever sub-divided and the rents were distributed amongst the co-sharers of the tenancy and as such, no amount of testimony or amicable partition can be taken into consideration to find the joint tenancy was sub-divided and jama was separated and thereby, the pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the tenancy. 

 15. It is true, out of the issues framed by the trial court the issues with regard to limitation and whether the pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the tenancy out of which the land was sold are raised as the most issues before me. No other issues was pressed for, so let me see whether the judgment and order of the court of appeal below are well founded in law as well as on facts. 

 17. Now, with regard to the locus standi of the petitioner. I have gone through the written objection filed by the purchaser. He has claimed that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the tenancy on three counts. Firstly after the death of Golam Mortuza Khan the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters amicably partitioned their inherited land and properties and they have been possessing their specific share independently and separately since then. Secondly, the land sold belongs to a separate Municipal holding than that of the holding where the petitioner has been living in and thirdly O.P.W. No. 5 wife of opposite party No. 3 Moslemuddin Khan admitted that after the death of her father-in-law the properties were separated amicably and now the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters staying in their separate and independent shares. The purchaser also adduced a D.C.R. Ext. Uma dated 29.02.88 issued by Assistant Tahsilder in respect of a Khatian No. 474/17/1. I have also seen the rent receipts marked as Ext. Uma (1) and Uma (2) showing payment of rents on 17.03.88 and 14.04.90. I have also perused a tax receipt Ext. Uma (3) issued by Dhaka Municipal Corporation showing payment of tax for the year 1988/89 and 1989/90 against holding No. 18/6/C in the name of Harunur Rashid. The purchaser examined himself as O.P.W. No. 1 and he testified that after the death of Golam Mortuza Khan the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters in 1974 amicably partitioned their inherited lands and properties. He also claimed to have got his purchased lands mutated in his name. In cross-examination, he testified that he could not remember whether he got the land mutated before the making of the application for pre-emption. But he was very categorical in deposing that he did not serve any notice upon the pre-emptor or his brothers and sisters because they were living in separate holdings. 

 18. There is no dispute, the property was originally owned and possessed by Golam Mortuza Khan. After his death the petitioner and his three brothers and six sisters opposite parties 3-11 inherited. They are living separately. Now, the question is whether in view of the above facts and the evidence on record can it be said, there was sub-division of the tenancy held by Golam Mortuza Khan and rents were distributed in accordance with law and thereby, the petitioners ceased to be a co-sharer in the joint tenancy and thereby, lost his right of pre-emption. 

 19. Section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 1950 has provided for sub-division of a holding and/or a joint tenancy and distribution of rents. Section 117 reads- 

 (c) for the purpose of subdivision of a joint tenancy for distribution of rent thereof, on an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants, direct, by order in writing such subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer tenants and distribution of rent thereof, including arrears of rent, if any, he may consider fair and equitable: 

 This provision is applicable for subdivision and distribution of rents in respect of all sorts of lands, agricultural and non-agricultural. Under the above provision, Revenue officer is given the power to subdivide a joint tenancy for the purpose of distribution of rents. Such jurisdiction can only be exercised upon an application made to him by one or more co-sharer tenants and after service of reasonable notice to the parties concerned to appear, and after hearing them. Following the provisions of the Section, the Revenue officer by an order in writing may direct subdivision of a joint tenancy amongst the co-sharer-tenants and distribution of rents thereof amongst them. 

 No such order of Revenue officer directing subdivision of the joint tenancy held by Golam Mortuza Khan and distributing the rents amongst the co-sharers i.e. the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters has been adduced in this case. The purchaser have categorically stated that before his getting the purchased land mutated, he did not serve any notice upon any heirs of said Golam Mortuza Khan Because, they are living in separate holding. Here, it must be noted that such authority for subdivision of a joint tenancy and the distribution of rents has not been given to any other authority including the Dhaka Municipal Corporation. Mutation of the Dhaka Municipal Corporation to be valid must be based on an order in writing of the Revenue officer concerned making the joint tenancy subdivided and rents distributed. It cannot be other way round. Separate holding number given by a Municipal Corporation cannot replace an order under Section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, so, the heirs of Golam Mortuza Khan must be held to be still enjoying the joint tenancy left by him. Similarly, no amicable partition among the co-sharers even if reached in writing nor even a decree passed in a partition suit allotting different shares to the co-sharers can substitute the order as mentioned in Section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In such view of the legal position as well as the factual position, the court of appeal below was perfectly justified in holding that the joint tenancy of Golam Murtoza Khan was never subdivided and the rents were never distributed amongst his heirs, pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters in accordance with law, and thereby, the pre-emptor did not cease to be a co-sharer in the Joint tenancy left by him. Accordingly, the pre-emptor, Eklas Hossain Khan is a co-sharer in the joint tenancy left by Golam Mortuza Khan. 

 20. In the case of M.A. Rouf Vs. Ahmuda Khatun, 33 DLR (AD) 323, it was clearly held, any subdivision without notice upon co-sharer of a joint tenancy would not affect the right of pre-emption. Moreover, even if a mutation or subdivision is obtained lawfully during the pendency of a proceeding for pre-emption that must be hit by the doctrine of lies pendent under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In this case, the purchaser did not adduce any evidence to show when the purchaser got the purchased land mutated in his name. But, Exts Uma series clearly show, those were issued during the pendency of the proceeding for pre-emption. If it is so, such mutation or subdivision is not based on any lawful order of a Revenue officer. Because, the order admittedly obtained without service of notice upon the pre-emptor and his brothers and sisters, must be also hit by the doctrine of lies pendent under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In the case of Begum Aisa Rahman Vs. Abdul Basir Bhuiyan, 26 DLR (SC) 58 it was held, subdivision of a holding without notice, on a co-sharer, does not defeat the right of a co-sharer of pre-emption. In the case of Begum Khodeja Akter Vs. Hareza Khatun, 37 DLR (AD) 212 as referred by Mr. N. H. Khondker for the purchaser, the case was remanded by the Appellate Division to the trial court to determine whether the jama was separated or not as none of the courts below held that a joint holding was subdivided or the rents were distributed. In the case of Sunil Krishna Banik Vs. Kailash Chandra Saha (1984) 4 BLD (AD) 320 the Appellate Division held that if an original co-sharer ceases to be a co-sharer of the joint tenancy he cannot apply for pre-emption. The person making the application for pre-emption must have a subsisting interest in the joint tenancy and such interest must continue au through the proceeding of pre-emption in order to be successful to get an order for pre-emption. 

 23. In the result, the Rule is discharged. No order as to costs. The judgment and order of the court of appeal below reversing those of the trial court are confirmed. The application pre-emption made by the predecessor of opposite party No. 1 and 2 under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of the impugned deed No. 617 executed on 18.02.88 and registered on 13.03.88 is allowed.
